analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare coinsurance for outpatient surgery center care at the hospital deductible amount.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill to cap Medicare co-pays for surgery center care was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 15, 2025, and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: When Medicare patients get surgery at a freestanding surgery center instead of a hospital, they can owe coinsurance that is higher than the full deductible for a hospital stay. This bill caps that charge at the inpatient hospital deductible and has Medicare pay surgeons' facilities the difference so providers do not lose money. It was introduced by a Republican and a Democrat and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat since May 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need outpatient surgery. Today, facility services at an ambulatory surgical center carry 20% coinsurance with no cap tied to the hospital deductible, so a patient can owe more for surgery-center care than the deductible for an inpatient hospital stay. The bill caps that charge at the inpatient deductible amount and reimburses the provider for the reduction, so the savings flow to patients rather than coming out of provider payments.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the coinsurance a Medicare patient owes for facility services at an ambulatory surgical center at the inpatient hospital deductible whenever the standard charge would be higher, effective for services on or after January 1, 2026.
Has the federal government pay the provider the amount of the reduction, so the cap does not cut what surgery centers are paid and patients keep their access to these facilities.

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare program. Every dollar of coinsurance relief for patients is reimbursed to the provider by CMS, which raises federal Medicare outlays for surgery-center services; the ultimate cost falls on taxpayers and the Medicare trust funds. Providers, including ambulatory surgical centers and hospital outpatient departments that compete with them, are held whole.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes Medicare pay providers the full amount of any coinsurance reduction, increasing federal Medicare spending with no offset identified in the bill text.
The cap is set at the inpatient hospital deductible, which is still a substantial out-of-pocket charge for many seniors, so it limits rather than eliminates the burden.
Capping patient cost-sharing while fully reimbursing providers removes price pressure at the point of care and could encourage more use of surgical services, adding to program costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient benefit is real and targeted: it fixes a genuine anomaly where Medicare patients can owe more for surgery-center care than for a hospital admission. The cost is higher federal Medicare spending, because the bill deliberately shields providers and shifts the bill to the program. The trade-off is reasonable for beneficiaries but adds to Medicare's finances without a pay-for.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it since May 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) introduced the Medicare Beneficiary Co-Pay Fairness Act on May 15, 2025.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, its only committee action to date.
One Senate Democrat has cosponsored the bill, making it a small bipartisan effort.
The bill would apply to services furnished on or after January 1, 2026, if enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet, since the bill has not been enacted. Medicare beneficiaries who need outpatient surgery are the group waiting on the cap; the outcome so far is simply inaction by the Finance Committee, which leaves the current higher coinsurance arrangement in place for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the bill just waits

for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap Medicare coinsurance for surgery-center facility services.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut, original co-sponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its Democratic co-lead.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for Medicare legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 15, 2025 and has taken no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is sponsored by a Republican (Cassidy) co-led with a Democrat (Blumenthal), with one additional Democratic cosponsor; no member has opposed it on the record.

industries.industry: Ambulatory surgical centers and outpatient surgery providers
industries.note: The bill keeps their payments whole by having Medicare reimburse the amount of the patient's coinsurance reduction, so their facility revenue is protected while their patients pay less. It could also modestly increase use of their services.

industries.industry: Federal Medicare program (trust funds and taxpayers)
industries.note: Medicare absorbs the cost of every coinsurance reduction as a new payment to providers, adding federal outlays with no offset in the bill.

analysis.trajectory: With only two sponsors, no committee action beyond referral, and no markup scheduled by the Finance Committee, the most likely path is that the bill sits through the end of the 119th Congress unless it is attached to a larger Medicare package. Bipartisan, budget-neutral-looking Medicare fixes sometimes ride along on broader health legislation, but that would require committee leadership to pick it up.
